morningSummary:
Wednesday, 18 November 2026 — Evening News. Updated at 18:00 Europe/Paris. Presented by Sophie Laurent.

GLOBAL LEAD — Gulf tensions have intensified. An ADNOC-linked vessel was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, leaving one crew member missing and 11 injured. Iran also widened attacks towards Kuwait and Bahrain; both reported interceptions. The security of commercial shipping and energy infrastructure remains a major concern.

APEC — Donald Trump is in Shenzhen. Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin have held talks, and a trilateral meeting involving Trump is expected Thursday. No three-leader agreement has yet been announced.

NIGERIA — The ADC says it has filed a 17-ground appeal against the judgment affecting its leadership and Atiku Abubakar's candidacy. It has asked the Court of Appeal to restrain INEC from changing party and candidate records while the appeal is pending. That request is not yet a court order.

AFRICA — South Africa has reprimanded Nigeria's High Commissioner Femi Fani-Kayode after a public broadcasting dispute. The UN says more than 2,230 civilians were killed in Sudan from January to October, including over 1,630 in drone strikes.

EUROPE — France's wage protests continue, with sharply different crowd estimates from the Interior Ministry and the CGT. Ukraine says a new strike damaged the Crimean Bridge; Russia has acknowledged damage, while some details remain disputed. US envoys are expected in Berlin Thursday for Ukraine talks.

MIDDLE EAST — A Saudi-led coalition has struck Houthi targets in Yemen as the wider region faces renewed military escalation.

BUSINESS AND TECHNOLOGY — Nvidia reported record revenue but its shares fell amid investor concern about the AI trade. Oil prices eased as US inventory data partly offset Gulf risk.

GLOBAL PICTURE — The evening is shaped by maritime security, great-power diplomacy, electoral due process, civilian protection and market uncertainty. RadiantWaves distinguishes confirmed developments from claims made by parties to conflicts or political disputes.

topStories.title: ADC files 17-ground appeal and asks Court of Appeal to protect candidate records
topStories.summary: The African Democratic Congress says it has filed a 17-ground appeal against the judgment affecting its leadership and Atiku Abubakar's candidacy. It has asked the Court of Appeal to restrain INEC from altering party and candidate records while the appeal is pending.
topStories.content: The ADC has disclosed a 17-ground appeal challenging the Federal High Court judgment delivered on 5 November in the leadership dispute involving the party. The party argues, among other points, that the trial court lacked jurisdiction and that the claimant's standing and disputed evidence were not properly assessed. It has also asked the Court of Appeal to preserve existing leadership records and candidate nomination particulars pending determination of the appeal. This is an application by the party, not confirmation that the appellate court has granted the requested restraint. The legal position remains subject to the courts' decisions and INEC's lawful obligations.

topStories.title: South Africa formally reprimands Nigeria's envoy after public broadcasting dispute
topStories.summary: South Africa's foreign ministry summoned Nigeria's High Commissioner Femi Fani-Kayode after a public dispute over coverage of his credentials ceremony. Pretoria says diplomatic concerns should be raised through official channels.
topStories.content: South Africa's Department of International Relations and Cooperation has formally reprimanded Nigeria's High Commissioner, Femi Fani-Kayode, after he complained that his introduction and speech were excluded from an SABC broadcast of his credentials ceremony. The Nigerian envoy disputed the handling of the event, while South African officials said diplomatic concerns should be channelled through the relevant institutions and foreign ministries. The disagreement comes amid wider sensitivities in bilateral relations, including concerns about attacks on foreign nationals. The public exchange is a diplomatic disagreement; it should not be confused with a formal rupture in relations.

topStories.title: UN verifies more than 2,230 civilian deaths in Sudan conflict through October
topStories.summary: The UN Human Rights Office says it verified at least 2,230 civilian deaths in Sudan between January and October 2026, including more than 1,630 linked to drone strikes. It warns the actual toll is likely higher.
topStories.content: A report by the UN Human Rights Office documents the devastating civilian impact of Sudan's war between the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces and allied armed groups. The UN says at least 2,230 civilians were killed from January to the end of October, with more than 1,630 deaths caused by drone strikes. Markets, hospitals, schools, fuel facilities, water sources and civilian vehicles have been hit. The Kordofan region accounted for more than two-thirds of verified civilian deaths. The UN says some violations may amount to war crimes and calls for accountability and protection of civilians. These are verified minimum figures, not a complete count of all deaths.

topStories.title: Ukraine says second strike damaged Crimean Bridge and collapsed a road span
topStories.summary: Ukraine's military and security services say a second strike damaged the Crimean Bridge and caused a road span to collapse. Russia has acknowledged damage and opened a terrorism investigation; independent confirmation of all Ukrainian claims remains limited.
topStories.content: Ukrainian officials say an operation on the Kerch, or Crimean, Bridge caused a section of the road span to fall into the water after a second night of strikes. Kyiv says the operation involved several weapons and services. Russian authorities confirmed damage, opened a terrorism case and said the bridge would be repaired. The bridge is a strategic road and rail link between Russia and occupied Crimea. Reporting on the precise extent of damage and the weapons used relies heavily on statements from the parties to the war, so those details should remain attributed rather than treated as independently established.

topStories.title: France protests: unions report more than 500,000 participants; Interior Ministry counts 146,000
topStories.summary: Demonstrations over wages and purchasing power continued on 17 November. The Interior Ministry counted 146,000 participants nationwide, while the CGT union claimed more than 500,000.
topStories.content: Public-sector unions called demonstrations demanding higher wages, joined by private-sector workers and young people. France's Interior Ministry estimated turnout at 146,000 nationwide, while the CGT union claimed more than 500,000. The marches were largely peaceful, but participation and the movement's momentum remain contested. Protesters say wages and public services have failed to keep pace with living costs. Union leaders are also seeking to influence the debate ahead of the April 2027 presidential election. The competing crowd figures should be attributed to their respective sources rather than presented as a single agreed count.

topStories.title: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner expected in Berlin for Ukraine talks
topStories.summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected in Berlin on Thursday to meet Ukrainian officials and European negotiators over security guarantees and reconstruction.
topStories.content: Reuters reports that the US plans to send Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Berlin for discussions with Ukrainian officials and European negotiators. The agenda is expected to include credible post-war security guarantees, Ukraine's economic recovery and preparations for further multilateral talks. The diplomatic effort follows recent contacts in Abu Dhabi and Moscow. Major differences remain: Russia is seeking control of the Donbas region, while Kyiv has resisted surrendering territory. The visit is expected, not yet completed, and no breakthrough has been announced.

topStories.title: Saudi-led coalition launches major strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen
topStories.summary: The Saudi-led coalition says it struck Houthi missile and drone facilities in Yemen. Houthi authorities reported deaths, while Saudi air defences said they intercepted missiles aimed at Riyadh.
topStories.content: The Associated Press reports that the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes against Houthi-held areas, targeting what it described as missile warehouses and drone workshops. Houthi authorities reported at least 17 deaths, including people killed at a factory in Hodeida. The Houthis also fired missiles towards Riyadh, which Saudi air defences said they intercepted. The casualty figures and descriptions of targets are reported claims from the parties and require independent verification. The escalation adds another layer of risk to an already volatile region and could affect shipping and humanitarian conditions.

topStories.title: Nvidia posts record revenue but AI-market anxiety weighs on shares
topStories.summary: Nvidia reported another quarter of record revenue and raised its guidance, but its shares fell as investors questioned the durability of the AI trade. Markets also watched oil and Federal Reserve signals.
topStories.content: The Wall Street Journal's market coverage reports that Nvidia announced record quarterly revenue and lifted its outlook, yet its shares declined and failed to lift broader technology stocks. Investors remain concerned about valuations and the scale of spending required to sustain artificial-intelligence growth. Other AI-linked companies also weakened, while traders awaited Federal Reserve minutes and further signals on interest rates. Oil prices eased as higher US inventories offset some of the risk premium from renewed Gulf fighting. A single trading session does not establish a long-term reversal in the AI sector, but it shows how sensitive markets have become to expectations.

topStories.title: Mozambique opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane goes on trial over post-election unrest
topStories.summary: Opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane has gone on trial over charges linked to protests after Mozambique's disputed 2024 election. He denies wrongdoing and says his demonstrations sought electoral transparency.
topStories.content: Mondlane is facing charges including terrorism-related offences, incitement and civil disobedience connected to unrest after the 2024 election. Prosecutors allege that his calls for demonstrations encouraged violence and disruption; Mondlane denies wrongdoing and says he challenged the election result through political protest. The case is being heard under tight security, with access to proceedings restricted. The charges carry potentially severe penalties if he is convicted. The trial is an important test of due process, political freedoms and public confidence in Mozambique's institutions.

topStories.title: Guinea sentences 224 people in crackdown on illegal gold mining
topStories.summary: A Guinean court has sentenced 224 people, including former regional officials and alleged illegal miners, over unauthorised gold-mining activities in Siguiri.
topStories.content: A court in Guinea has sentenced 224 people in a case involving illegal mining, environmental damage and water pollution. The defendants include 22 former regional administrators and 202 miners. The reported sentences form part of a government crackdown on unauthorised gold extraction in the Siguiri region. The operation has also been accompanied by protests and clashes, with reported deaths and injuries. The case highlights the challenge of protecting rivers and farmland while ensuring that enforcement is lawful, proportionate and does not punish people without fair hearings.

topStories.country: Philippines / United States / India / Japan / Australia
topStories.summary: Leaders of the Quad countries are meeting in Manila for the first leaders' gathering in more than two years, with maritime security, AI and critical minerals on the agenda.
topStories.content: The Quad grouping of the United States, India, Japan and Australia is holding a leaders' meeting in Manila. Discussions include maritime security, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and supply-chain resilience. The meeting comes as regional governments navigate strategic competition and seek to protect sea lanes and access to key technologies. The group is not a formal military alliance, and any commitments should be assessed from the official communique rather than assumed from the meeting itself.

topStories.title: ICJ expected to deliver ruling in The Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar
topStories.summary: The International Court of Justice is expected to issue its substantive ruling on Thursday in The Gambia's case alleging violations of the Genocide Convention against Myanmar. The judgment has not yet been delivered.
topStories.content: The case concerns allegations that Myanmar violated the 1948 Genocide Convention in its treatment of the Rohingya. The Gambia brought the case at the ICJ, which has previously ordered provisional measures requiring Myanmar to prevent acts covered by the convention and preserve evidence. A ruling is expected on Thursday, 19 November, but it has not yet been issued. The judgment will address state responsibility under international law; it is distinct from individual criminal prosecutions. The outcome will be closely watched by Rohingya survivors, human-rights organisations and governments considering accountability measures.

topStories.whyItMatters: The decision could clarify the obligations of states under the Genocide Convention and shape future accountability efforts.
topStories.whatHappensNext: Follow the Court's official judgment and distinguish findings on state responsibility from criminal convictions of individuals.

articles.title: Iran-Gulf escalation: ADNOC-linked vessel attacked as Bahrain and Kuwait report interceptions
articles.summary: An ADNOC-linked vessel was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz, leaving one crew member missing and 11 injured. Iran also widened attacks towards Kuwait and Bahrain; both countries said their air defences intercepted threats.
articles.content: The Associated Press reports that an Abu Dhabi state oil company vessel was attacked in the Strait of Hormuz. Eleven crew members were injured and one remained missing as search and rescue continued. Separately, Iran said it targeted military systems at Ali Al Salem Air Base in Kuwait; Kuwait and Bahrain reported intercepting incoming threats. These developments follow US strikes on Iranian military sites and continued confrontation over the naval blockade and the strait. Claims about targets and damage must be attributed to the parties making them. The immediate concern is the safety of crews, commercial shipping and energy infrastructure across the Gulf.

articles.title: APEC: Trump, Xi and Putin prepare for Thursday trilateral meeting in Shenzhen
articles.summary: Donald Trump is in China for the APEC summit. Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin have held talks, while a three-leader meeting is expected on Thursday; no trilateral outcome has been announced.
articles.content: At the APEC summit in Shenzhen, Xi Jinping called for open trade and more equitable growth, while Vladimir Putin criticised Western sanctions and export controls. Donald Trump has arrived in China. Reuters reports that a meeting between Trump and Putin is expected on the sidelines, alongside a planned trilateral discussion with Xi on Thursday. The leaders may address trade, Ukraine, Iran, artificial intelligence and nuclear security. The meeting has not yet taken place, and no agreement should be presumed. Other Asia-Pacific economies will be watching whether the major powers reduce tensions or deepen strategic competition.

articles.title: ADC files 17-ground appeal and asks Court of Appeal to protect candidate records
articles.summary: The African Democratic Congress says it has filed a 17-ground appeal against the judgment affecting its leadership and Atiku Abubakar's candidacy. It has asked the Court of Appeal to restrain INEC from altering party and candidate records while the appeal is pending.
articles.content: The ADC has disclosed a 17-ground appeal challenging the Federal High Court judgment delivered on 5 November in the leadership dispute involving the party. The party argues, among other points, that the trial court lacked jurisdiction and that the claimant's standing and disputed evidence were not properly assessed. It has also asked the Court of Appeal to preserve existing leadership records and candidate nomination particulars pending determination of the appeal. This is an application by the party, not confirmation that the appellate court has granted the requested restraint. The legal position remains subject to the courts' decisions and INEC's lawful obligations.

articles.title: South Africa formally reprimands Nigeria's envoy after public broadcasting dispute
articles.summary: South Africa's foreign ministry summoned Nigeria's High Commissioner Femi Fani-Kayode after a public dispute over coverage of his credentials ceremony. Pretoria says diplomatic concerns should be raised through official channels.
articles.content: South Africa's Department of International Relations and Cooperation has formally reprimanded Nigeria's High Commissioner, Femi Fani-Kayode, after he complained that his introduction and speech were excluded from an SABC broadcast of his credentials ceremony. articles.title: UN verifies more than 2,230 civilian deaths in Sudan conflict through October
articles.summary: The UN Human Rights Office says it verified at least 2,230 civilian deaths in Sudan between January and October 2026, including more than 1,630 linked to drone strikes. It warns the actual toll is likely higher.
articles.content: A report by the UN Human Rights Office documents the devastating civilian impact of Sudan's war between the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces and allied armed groups. The UN says at least 2,230 civilians were killed from January to the end of October, with more than 1,630 deaths caused by drone strikes. Markets, hospitals, schools, fuel facilities, water sources and civilian vehicles have been hit. The Kordofan region accounted for more than two-thirds of verified civilian deaths. The UN says some violations may amount to war crimes and calls for accountability and protection of civilians. These are verified minimum figures, not a complete count of all deaths.

articles.imageNote: Contextual image for this report; not represented as a photograph of the specific event unless stated.

articles.title: Ukraine says second strike damaged Crimean Bridge and collapsed a road span
articles.summary: Ukraine's military and security services say a second strike damaged the Crimean Bridge and caused a road span to collapse. Russia has acknowledged damage and opened a terrorism investigation; independent confirmation of all Ukrainian claims remains limited.
articles.content: Ukrainian officials say an operation on the Kerch, or Crimean, Bridge caused a section of the road span to fall into the water after a second night of strikes. Kyiv says the operation involved several weapons and services. Russian authorities confirmed damage, opened a terrorism case and said the bridge would be repaired. The bridge is a strategic road and rail link between Russia and occupied Crimea. Reporting on the precise extent of damage and the weapons used relies heavily on statements from the parties to the war, so those details should remain attributed rather than treated as independently established.

articles.title: France protests: unions report more than 500,000 participants; Interior Ministry counts 146,000
articles.summary: Demonstrations over wages and purchasing power continued on 17 November. The Interior Ministry counted 146,000 participants nationwide, while the CGT union claimed more than 500,000.
articles.content: Public-sector unions called demonstrations demanding higher wages, joined by private-sector workers and young people. France's Interior Ministry estimated turnout at 146,000 nationwide, while the CGT union claimed more than 500,000. The marches were largely peaceful, but participation and the movement's momentum remain contested. Protesters say wages and public services have failed to keep pace with living costs. Union leaders are also seeking to influence the debate ahead of the April 2027 presidential election. The competing crowd figures should be attributed to their respective sources rather than presented as a single agreed count.

articles.title: US envoys Witkoff and Kushner expected in Berlin for Ukraine talks
articles.summary: US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected in Berlin on Thursday to meet Ukrainian officials and European negotiators over security guarantees and reconstruction.
articles.content: Reuters reports that the US plans to send Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Berlin for discussions with Ukrainian officials and European negotiators. The agenda is expected to include credible post-war security guarantees, Ukraine's economic recovery and preparations for further multilateral talks. The diplomatic effort follows recent contacts in Abu Dhabi and Moscow. Major differences remain: Russia is seeking control of the Donbas region, while Kyiv has resisted surrendering territory. The visit is expected, not yet completed, and no breakthrough has been announced.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition launches major strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition says it struck Houthi missile and drone facilities in Yemen. Houthi authorities reported deaths, while Saudi air defences said they intercepted missiles aimed at Riyadh.
articles.content: The Associated Press reports that the Saudi-led coalition launched airstrikes against Houthi-held areas, targeting what it described as missile warehouses and drone workshops. The escalation adds another layer of risk to an already volatile region and could affect shipping and humanitarian conditions.

articles.title: Nvidia posts record revenue but AI-market anxiety weighs on shares
articles.summary: Nvidia reported another quarter of record revenue and raised its guidance, but its shares fell as investors questioned the durability of the AI trade. Markets also watched oil and Federal Reserve signals.
articles.content: The Wall Street Journal's market coverage reports that Nvidia announced record quarterly revenue and lifted its outlook, yet its shares declined and failed to lift broader technology stocks. Investors remain concerned about valuations and the scale of spending required to sustain artificial-intelligence growth. Other AI-linked companies also weakened, while traders awaited Federal Reserve minutes and further signals on interest rates. Oil prices eased as higher US inventories offset some of the risk premium from renewed Gulf fighting. A single trading session does not establish a long-term reversal in the AI sector, but it shows how sensitive markets have become to expectations.

articles.title: Mozambique opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane goes on trial over post-election unrest
articles.summary: Opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane has gone on trial over charges linked to protests after Mozambique's disputed 2024 election. He denies wrongdoing and says his demonstrations sought electoral transparency.
articles.content: Mondlane is facing charges including terrorism-related offences, incitement and civil disobedience connected to unrest after the 2024 election. Prosecutors allege that his calls for demonstrations encouraged violence and disruption; Mondlane denies wrongdoing and says he challenged the election result through political protest. The case is being heard under tight security, with access to proceedings restricted. The charges carry potentially severe penalties if he is convicted. The trial is an important test of due process, political freedoms and public confidence in Mozambique's institutions.

articles.title: Guinea sentences 224 people in crackdown on illegal gold mining
articles.summary: A Guinean court has sentenced 224 people, including former regional officials and alleged illegal miners, over unauthorised gold-mining activities in Siguiri.
articles.content: A court in Guinea has sentenced 224 people in a case involving illegal mining, environmental damage and water pollution. The defendants include 22 former regional administrators and 202 miners. The reported sentences form part of a government crackdown on unauthorised gold extraction in the Siguiri region. The operation has also been accompanied by protests and clashes, with reported deaths and injuries. The case highlights the challenge of protecting rivers and farmland while ensuring that enforcement is lawful, proportionate and does not punish people without fair hearings.

articles.country: Philippines / United States / India / Japan / Australia
articles.summary: Leaders of the Quad countries are meeting in Manila for the first leaders' gathering in more than two years, with maritime security, AI and critical minerals on the agenda.
articles.content: The Quad grouping of the United States, India, Japan and Australia is holding a leaders' meeting in Manila. Discussions include maritime security, critical minerals, artificial intelligence and supply-chain resilience. The meeting comes as regional governments navigate strategic competition and seek to protect sea lanes and access to key technologies. The group is not a formal military alliance, and any commitments should be assessed from the official communique rather than assumed from the meeting itself.

articles.title: ICJ expected to deliver ruling in The Gambia's genocide case against Myanmar
articles.summary: The International Court of Justice is expected to issue its substantive ruling on Thursday in The Gambia's case alleging violations of the Genocide Convention against Myanmar. The judgment has not yet been delivered.
articles.content: The case concerns allegations that Myanmar violated the 1948 Genocide Convention in its treatment of the Rohingya. The Gambia brought the case at the ICJ, which has previously ordered provisional measures requiring Myanmar to prevent acts covered by the convention and preserve evidence. A ruling is expected on Thursday, 19 November, but it has not yet been issued. The judgment will address state responsibility under international law; it is distinct from individual criminal prosecutions. The outcome will be closely watched by Rohingya survivors, human-rights organisations and governments considering accountability measures.

articles.imageNote: Contextual image for this report; not represented as a photograph of the specific event unless stated.
articles.whyItMatters: The decision could clarify the obligations of states under the Genocide Convention and shape future accountability efforts.
articles.whatHappensNext: Follow the Court's official judgment and distinguish findings on state responsibility from criminal convictions of individuals.
articles.label: INTERNATIONAL LAW

nigeriaNews.title: ADC files 17-ground appeal and asks Court of Appeal to protect candidate records
nigeriaNews.summary: The African Democratic Congress says it has filed a 17-ground appeal against the judgment affecting its leadership and Atiku Abubakar's candidacy. It has asked the Court of Appeal to restrain INEC from altering party and candidate records while the appeal is pending.
nigeriaNews.content: The ADC has disclosed a 17-ground appeal challenging the Federal High Court judgment delivered on 5 November in the leadership dispute involving the party. The party argues, among other points, that the trial court lacked jurisdiction and that the claimant's standing and disputed evidence were not properly assessed. It has also asked the Court of Appeal to preserve existing leadership records and candidate nomination particulars pending determination of the appeal. businessNews.content: The Wall Street Journal's market coverage reports that Nvidia announced record quarterly revenue and lifted its outlook, yet its shares declined and failed to lift broader technology stocks. Investors remain concerned about valuations and the scale of spending required to sustain artificial-intelligence growth. Other AI-linked companies also weakened, while traders awaited Federal Reserve minutes and further signals on interest rates. Oil prices eased as higher US inventories offset some of the risk premium from renewed Gulf fighting. A single trading session does not establish a long-term reversal in the AI sector, but it shows how sensitive markets have become to expectations.

editorial.title: Political disputes must be settled by evidence and due process
editorial.imageAlt: Nigeria political and legal process context image
editorial.summary: The ADC appeal is now part of a legal process. INEC, political parties and the courts should act transparently while respecting due process.
editorial.content: The ADC's 17-ground appeal raises questions that must be resolved by the courts, not by political pressure or online speculation. The party's request to preserve its candidate records is an application, not an order already granted. INEC should comply with valid court directions, explain its actions clearly and avoid prejudging the appeal. All political actors deserve equal treatment under the law, and voters deserve certainty before the 2027 election timetable advances.

analysis.title: Why attacks around Hormuz can affect economies far from the Gulf
analysis.imageAlt: Gulf shipping and maritime security illustration
analysis.summary: Threats to vessels can raise insurance, freight and energy costs even without a formal closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
analysis.content: The latest incident involving an ADNOC-linked vessel demonstrates how insecurity can affect commercial shipping. Ship operators may reroute, delay voyages or face higher insurance premiums. Energy traders also price in the possibility of supply disruption. Import-dependent economies in Asia, Europe and Africa can feel the impact through fuel, transport and production costs. The scale of the effect depends on how long the risk persists, whether traffic is disrupted and whether diplomatic efforts reduce tensions.

analysis.title: Sudan's drone war shows why civilian protection must be central to diplomacy
analysis.summary: The UN's verified casualty figures underline the impact of drone attacks on markets, hospitals, fuel supplies and other civilian infrastructure.
analysis.content: The UN's latest figures are a minimum verified count, not the full human cost. Drone attacks have affected essential services and livelihoods far from front lines. Humanitarian access, protection of civilian infrastructure, independent investigations and accountability should be priorities in any diplomatic initiative. The parties to the conflict must comply with international humanitarian law regardless of their military objectives.

beyondStatement.title: An appeal is not the same as a court order
beyondStatement.imageAlt: Nigeria court and party leadership dispute context
beyondStatement.summary: The ADC has filed an appeal and asked for interim protection of candidate records. The request must not be reported as an order already granted.
beyondStatement.content: The distinction matters. A party can file grounds of appeal and ask the Court of Appeal for interim relief, but the court must decide whether to grant that relief. Until an order is made, the legal position should be described precisely. Readers should look for the court's actual ruling and any official INEC response.

beyondStatement.title: Verified minimums are not the full toll
beyondStatement.summary: The UN's verified civilian death toll in Sudan is a minimum count based on documented cases; the actual toll is likely higher.
beyondStatement.content: Conflict casualty figures often change as investigators gain access to affected areas. The UN's 2,230 figure is a verified minimum for January to October 2026. It should not be presented as a complete final total. Accurate reporting preserves the time period, verification method and warning about undercounting.

publicInterestFeature.title: Sudan's civilian toll: the human cost behind the numbers
publicInterestFeature.imageAlt: Sudan humanitarian crisis and civilian protection, contextual illustration
publicInterestFeature.summary: The UN's latest verified figures show the impact of drone attacks on hospitals, markets, fuel supplies and essential services.
publicInterestFeature.content: At least 2,230 civilians were verified killed in Sudan between January and October 2026, according to the UN Human Rights Office. More than 1,630 deaths were linked to drone strikes. The UN says the actual toll is likely higher. The report documents attacks affecting markets, hospitals, schools, fuel facilities, water sources and civilian vehicles. The figures are not just a measure of battlefield violence: they describe damage to the systems that keep families alive. Protection of civilians, safe humanitarian access and accountability must be central to any effort to end the conflict.
